736.t: Opinion of Ken Burns's Jazz series
736.s: Bash enjoyed Burns's series, whose two episodes were edited by Sandra Christie, and does not begrudge his success.
736.ch: Mary Lou Williams and Ken Burns
736.q: She edited two of the programs in his series. I actually enjoyed the series. I mean clearly there are some figures left out, but you can’t do it all. And I’m glad actually he left out Mary Lou to an extent. He mentioned her, so that means that somebody else has to take up that torch. I think there…

914.t: Ken Burns and his jazz series
914.s: Crohn recalls being asked to lunch by Burns' office, and criticises the Bird clip cut and the reliance on Crouch and Marsalis.
914.q: Yes. They even came to me. Somebody from Ken Burns’ office called me up and said, “Let’s have lunch.” And I said ooh, maybe there’s something in it for me. And on the phone I said I’d love to — if you need someone to produce some segments I’d love to do it. “Oh no, we have people to do that.” They…

668.t: Jazz at a standstill and Marsalis's Jelly Roll Morton concert
668.s: Davern thinks jazz is decomposing; he was outraged by a repertory concert of Morton and by alternate takes issued in place of definitive ones.
668.ch: Influences and the state of jazz
668.q: I think you said it, it’s at a standstill. It’s perhaps in a state perhaps of decomposition because the other night I heard, again, airport to home and scan the airwaves, I heard a concert from I think it was either Carnegie Hall or Lincoln Center with Wynton Marsalis and they were playing the…

915.t: Reaction to the Ken Burns Jazz series and Iowa audiences
915.s: Gordon defends the Ken Burns series for bringing jazz to the masses despite complaints about omissions, citing rural Iowa audiences on a Lincoln Center residency.
915.q: I’ve seen very little of it. But what I have seen I’ve enjoyed it. I’ve enjoyed it. Well I don’t know if you’re asking me what I think about it, but I’m getting ready to tell you.

59.t: Ken Burns's Jazz series and the Charlie Parker clip
59.s: Hyman praises the publicity but notes omissions, and tells how his own solo with Parker was cut.
59.q: Oh you don’t need my commentary on Ken Burns. I’ve read everything that’s floating around on the Web and various other magazine and newspaper articles. I think it’s marvelous that there is such a thing and that the publicity has been given to jazz to a degree that none of us ever would have…

618.s: He saw part of it, liked learning about Armstrong, but wished it had been more balanced.
618.q: You know I didn’t see that whole documentary. I saw some of the early ones and enjoyed learning so much about Louis Armstrong. A lot of stuff I didn’t really know. So I was really pleased and I saw that as a big plus. From talking to my musical colleagues that apparently he left the last 50 years…

105.t: Ken Burns's Jazz, and the state of jazz history
105.s: Hamilton says the Ken Burns series was poor and mentioned him only for curly hair, and he says he does his own thing.
105.q: That sucked. I read in this book, -- you know what he said about me, the only thing he said about me, Chico Hamilton had curly hair.

371.t: Ken Burns's Jazz omitting the Lafayette Theater
371.s: Teddie and Hank feel the documentary did not go deep enough and left out the Lafayette Theater era.
371.q: Would you say that they did a complete story on jazz? They didn't go far back enough I thought. Nothing was mentioned about the Lafayette.

704.t: Ken Burns's Jazz and the hurt to Benny Carter
704.s: Jones recalls turning down Ken Burns's three-year project, which went with Stanley Crouch instead, and says the last two hours crammed in 40 people and hurt Benny Carter.
704.q: I used to be like that, because I was the hard-core, black-belt, bebop mentality, and anything that didn’t hit that thing was da-da-da-da-da, forget about it. I’m not like that. It ain’t going to be like that. Not if you can do it. If you can break – you can do anything you can when you can break…

228.s: McLean refused to talk about Coltrane for Burns, disliked the choice of consultants like Wynton Marsalis, and noted missing voices like Benny Carter.
228.ch: Hartford, prison, theater and the Collective
228.q: I can’t tell you that. I can’t remember. I didn’t give him too much more than – except what you saw.
